name: Gupta Empire
summary: Often called India’s “classical age”, known for advances in mathematics (decimal place value, zero), astronomy and Sanskrit literature.

knownFor.label: Zero and decimal place value
knownFor.note: Written place-value numerals including zero developed in this era.

location.value: Northern and central India, ruled from Pataliputra (and later Ayodhya).

terrain.value: The Ganges plain as the core, extending to central India and parts of the west.

resources.value: Fertile farmland, iron, and silk, pepper, pearls and ivory for export.

disasters.value: A great flood in the mid-6th century is mentioned in Wikipedia, but it is marked as needing a citation.

population.value: About 75 million in the 5th century (Wikipedia infobox).

urbanisation.value: Pataliputra revived. Ujjain and other cities flourished.

disease.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

migration.value: Huna (Hun) invasions from Central Asia in the late 5th century.

tradeRoutes.value: Exports of silk, pepper, pearls and ivory to the Sasanian and Byzantine empires and Southeast Asia.

wealth.value: No GDP estimate. Often described as a prosperous age.

moneyAndTax.value: Fine gold dinara coins, plus silver and copper coins and cowries.

inequality.value: A varna (caste) system. Historians debate how rigid caste became.

governmentType.value: A monarchy under a “Maharajadhiraja” (great king of kings), with provinces, districts and local councils.

keyRulers.value: Chandragupta I (crowned 320 CE). Samudragupta (c. 335–375). Chandragupta II (380–415). Kumaragupta I (415–455). Skandagupta (455–467). Vishnugupta (last, c. 540–550).

succession.value: Hereditary. The succession after Samudragupta (Ramagupta) is disputed.

institutions.value: Provinces (bhukti) and districts (vishaya) with councils. The Chinese pilgrim Faxian reported mild punishments (mostly fines).

stability.value: The “Pax Gupta” of the 4th–5th centuries. Pressure from the Pushyamitras and Hunas in the mid-5th century.

armyAndTech.value: Cavalry, elephants and archers, and iron weapons.

majorWars.value: Samudragupta’s campaigns. Chandragupta II’s defeat of the Western Kshatrapas (Sakas) by about 409. Skandagupta’s repulse of the Huns (c. 455), then later Hun invasions.

territoryChange.value: About 1.7–3.5 million km² at its height (Wikipedia gives a low and a high estimate).

alliancesRivals.value: The Vakatakas (allied by marriage). Rivals: the Sakas, the Hunas (Kidarites, Alchon Huns) and Yashodharman of Malwa.

inventions.value: Aryabhata (499) used place-value numbers and calculated pi to four decimal places, and his successors developed the concept of zero. The iron pillar of Delhi. Early chess (chaturanga).

scienceEducation.value: Scholars Aryabhata and Varahamihira (astronomy, mathematics), and medicine. Nalanda university was founded (traditionally under Kumaragupta I).

openness.value: Received Chinese pilgrims (Faxian), and traded and exchanged ideas widely.

religion.value: Vaishnavism (official) and the revival of Hinduism, alongside Buddhism and Jainism.

languageWriting.value: Sanskrit (literary and academic) and Prakrit (everyday), in the Gupta script.

artsArchitecture.value: Kalidasa’s plays and poetry, the Sarnath Buddha statues, early Hindu temples, and Ajanta cave paintings (partly).

socialStructure.value: A four-fold varna system, with occupations not always rigid. Some historians say caste hardened in this period.

sharedIdentity.value: Often called India’s “Golden Age” (this label is disputed by some historians).

neighbours.value: The Sasanian Empire, the Huns, the Vakatakas, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asian kingdoms.

ideasReligions.value: Indian mathematics (decimal numbers), astronomy and religion spread to Southeast Asia and, via Arabs, to the world.

colonisation.value: Expanded by conquest and made many local rulers into tributaries.

riseSignals.value: Chandragupta I’s marriage alliance with the Licchavis, and Samudragupta’s conquests.

peakPeriod.value: The reigns of Samudragupta, Chandragupta II and Kumaragupta I (c. 335–455).

declineSignals.value: Hun invasions, feudatories breaking away, the cost of war, and loss of territory.

outcome.value: Fragmentation. The empire faded by the mid-6th century (last inscription 542/543) into regional kingdoms such as the Maukharis and Pushyabhutis.

sources.value: Inscriptions (the Allahabad Pillar), coins, Sanskrit literature and Faxian’s travel account. Checked against Wikipedia on 6 Nov 2026. See also Thapar (2002).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate. Dates vary (Wikipedia: c. 240–579; the imperial period from 320). The “Golden Age” label and Kalidasa’s dates are debated.
